This is a really good question, and not an easy one. First off, increasing genetic diversity of crops, either through natural cross-breading, trait selection, or other artificial means that don't rely on chemicals for resistance to crop pests, fungus's, microbes, or other intrusive artifacts, is needed. And, I realize that for the artificial variety, companies need strong, but limited IP control for it to be profitable. But it is necessary. Also, desertification isn't something that can be solved by GM crops. It is also something that should be separated from terms like exhaustion and chemical abuse. Desertification is the destruction of crop land due to strip-agricultural techniques. These can be solved traditionally. Look at Myanmar for a perfect example of strip-agriculture. Neither traditional nor GM crops will make up for lackluster crop sustainability initiatives.

As far as a proposal, I say look toward sustainability efforts in extreme environmental regions for answers to many Western issues. Sad really because the idea behind all this green tech is great, it's just people use a shit load of energy to do it, and then say "oooh I saved a tonne of CO2". But then forget to realise the extra energy used, in effect, emitted several tonnes.

Pointless, but interesting regardless. Thanks OP.

EDIT: I think I want to add a little something. Although the actual process of "personal agriculture" is still, on average, at a loss compared to intensive farming (giant fields, fertiliser, etc.), I think that thinking about these processes is still valuable. It seems to help make people less wasteful and more mindful about the biosphere of the Earth, and make them less of a destructive component of humanity.

It still is a solidily-inescapable reality that we have grown too large to rely soley on "poop and love" to feed people.

Heck, we do all this intensive stuff, and even then we can only feed half the world with a healthy amount of food.

Yes, time, energy and effort are required to grow fruits and vegetables. For the hobbyist like myself however the time, energy and effort required is a sacrifice some are willing to make and the positives far outweigh any potential negatives IMO.

While it may not be revolutionary I do believe that people in urban centres should be encouraged to grow if possible, even if it is for a hobby.
